title: The Middle-Length Sayings
hookLine: 152 discourses of middle length; we read highlights in order, with Chalmers' translation

lines: A RAFT, A SAW, A WATER SNAKE.
cards: Some books you read cover to cover. Some you live in. For the next hundred and twenty-one days, this path lives in one: the Majjhima Nikaya, the Middle-Length Sayings of the Buddha.
Not every page, but its highlights, in order. A man alone in a forest at night, waiting for fear to arrive. A raft.
A saw. A water snake. A murderer who becomes a monk.
A man shot with a poisoned arrow who won't let the doctor touch it until he knows who fired it.

teach.b: Nikaya means a collection, a group. Majjhima means middle.
The discourse basket of the Pali canon holds five nikayas, sorted partly by length: the Long Discourses, the Middle-Length, the Connected, the Numbered, and a collection of shorter books.
The middle one holds a hundred and fifty-two discourses, in three sets of fifty, with fifty-two in the last. Mostly the Buddha speaks, but not only. Sariputta teaches.
Mahakaccana unpacks a riddle. The nun Dhammadinna answers hard questions.

teach.h: SARIPUTTA, KINGS, A NUN, A MURDERER.
teach.b: Kings, brahmins, Jain ascetics and wandering philosophers walk through, and a murderer named Angulimala.
Some well-known teachings live here: the foundations of mindfulness in MN 10, the raft in MN 22, the noble search in MN 26, the poisoned arrow in MN 63, Angulimala in MN 86.

Tradition says these discourses were recited together after the Buddha's death and carried for centuries by memory, by monks who specialized in chanting particular collections, before being written down in Sri Lanka around the first century BCE.
In English, Lord Chalmers' translation, Further Dialogues of the Buddha, appeared in the 1920s; these lessons lean on it and on the Pali, mostly retold. And the book has the feel of a real world.
People argue. People misunderstand. Some walk away unconvinced, and the reciters kept those too.

how: In Theravada countries the Majjhima Nikaya is studied in monasteries and recited in Pali, and many lay Buddhists read it in translation; its suttas are often the texts teachers return to for instruction.

o: the Middle-Length Sayings, a collection of discourses
a later commentary explaining the suttas
a book of monastic rules for monks and nuns

games.q: match the words and the discourses.

s: in three sets of fifty, with fifty-two in the last.
every discourse in it is spoken by the Buddha
Sariputta, Mahakaccana and the nun Dhammadinna teach too.
it was written down during the Buddha's lifetime
tradition says it was carried by memory and written down in Sri Lanka around the first century BCE.

games.q: you're a monk a century after the Buddha. there are no written books of his teaching. how do the discourses survive?
o: monks memorize and chant them, collection by collection
each monk writes his own version
games.why: tradition says reciters specialized in particular collections and chanted them together, generation after generation, until they were written down.

practice: Read these titles slowly: the root of all things, all the taints, heirs in the teaching, fear and dread, the simile of the cloth, the simile of the saw, the water snake, the anthill. Let one catch you, without asking why.
Then rest with the breath, and let that one title sit beside you.

wordCard.voice: Majjhima Nikaya. The Middle-Length Sayings: a hundred and fifty-two discourses, our book for the next stretch of the path.

orig.note: Pali majjhima-nikāya: the middle collection, the Middle-Length Sayings.

carryVoice: Your line: the middle length. A book to live in, a little at a time. Day four hundred one, and a new block.

sources.ref: Lord Chalmers, Further Dialogues of the Buddha (1926–27)
